vignette: Mrs. Lee is a 76-year-old South Eastern Asian woman who has been working as a mechanic for over four decades. Her current situation stems from an intense period of stalking that began about six months ago when she was walking home one evening. She had grown accustomed to the quiet streets near her workplace, but on this night, she noticed someone following her steps. Over the next few weeks, the stalker's presence became increasingly menacing, culminating in a threatening encounter where the individual cornered her in an alley. Since then, Mrs. Lee has been living with the haunting memories of that event. The odors of soil and outdoor scents now serve as potent triggers for her. The last time she was working on a car near freshly tilled earth, the smell instantly transported her back to that alley, making it difficult for her to focus. She had come to believe that any olfactory cue reminiscent of that place would bring those terrifying moments rushing back in full detail. This hyper-awareness extended even further; whenever she felt happy or relaxed, she found herself immediately on edge, fearing the blissful state might lure out the stalker. Mrs. Lee's hypervigilance is relentless. She frequently looks behind her to check if someone is following her and feels superalert or watchful even inside her own home. This constant monitoring has led her to push the memory of the traumatic event away before she can fully recall it, which in turn makes it difficult for her to explain what happened clearly. "When I try to recount what occurred," she confides, "I lose track and cannot finish the story." The memory of that frightening night feels like a series of photographs flashing through her mind. She is certain that if she dwells on those images too deeply, she will be unable to stop them from flooding back in full detail, which terrifies her most. The more she tries to avoid these memories, the sharper and more vivid they become, creating a self-reinforcing cycle. Her hypervigilance has also affected how she interacts with others. She became increasingly isolated, avoiding social gatherings that might expose her to the smells of earth or situations where she feels less vigilant. Her husband notices that she is often on guard even when at home, which affects their relationship and his peace of mind as well. The event itself was so traumatic that any sensory cue, whether olfactory or emotional, can trigger intense flashbacks. For instance, just the scent of damp earth from a rainy day at work sends her reeling back to that alley, and she finds herself looking over her shoulder multiple times throughout the day. This heightened state of alertness makes it nearly impossible for her to relax. Mrs. Lee's hypervigilance has created a feedback loop where her constant threat monitoring exacerbates her memory issues. She frequently pushes away the memories when they start to surface, only to have them return in fragments that she cannot fully explain. This cycle is exhausting and debilitating, leaving her feeling isolated and anxious. What finally brought Mrs. Lee to seek help was an incident at work where a colleague's perfume triggered such intense distress that she had to leave abruptly. She is most afraid of losing control or not being able to protect herself in the future but hopes for relief from the constant fear and better management of her memories so she can regain some sense of normalcy in her daily life.
